S&P 500 Price Target Accuracy & Calibration Report

An Empirical Study of Analyst Consensus and Forecast Errors for the Top 10 Mega-Cap Companies over the Last 10 Years (2016-2026)

📊 Moderately Poor Accuracy

Analyst forecast error (MAPE) averages 28% across S&P 500 leaders. Price targets act as broad expected ranges rather than precise point estimates.

~28.0% Avg MAPE

🚀 Underestimation (Pessimism) Bias

For fast-growing tech leaders (NVDA, META, AAPL), consensus targets systematically underestimated growth, resulting in hit rates of 60% to 84%.

60% - 84% Hit Rates

📉 Near-Zero Predictive Power

Expected return forecasts explain less than 3.5% of the variance in realized returns. Target revisions function primarily as lagging momentum-chasing indicators.

R² < 3.5%

1. Systematic Bias Distribution

This chart plots the density of analyst forecast errors across all 10 companies. An error of 0% represents a perfect forecast.

  • Underestimation for Leaders: The average forecast error is negative for mega-caps like NVDA (-24.7%) and META (-21.1%), indicating that analyst targets were consistently behind the actual returns.
  • Narrower Error Spread: Split-adjustment removes the massive unadjusted error outliers, centering the forecast distribution near the true economic bounds.

2. Return Calibration Scatter Plot

If targets were perfectly calibrated, expected returns would equal actual returns (falling on the dotted 1:1 line). OLS regression shows the empirical reality.

  • Flat Regression Slope: The regression beta coefficient is only ~0.14, showing that a 10% expected return on a target price translates to a mere 1.4% actual return.
  • Low R-squared: Very low explanatory power (R² < 3.5%) indicates target return calculations have almost zero forecast value for future gains.

3. Calibration Curve by Quintiles

We group expected returns into 5 quintiles to evaluate if realized returns rise monotonically with analyst expectations.

  • Decoupling: Actual returns do not follow expected returns in a linear relationship. The lowest quintile can often perform similarly to or better than higher expected quintiles, showing a lack of calibration.

4. 12-Month Projected Consensus vs. Price

Here, the consensus target series is shifted forward by 365 days to align it with the actual target date it predicts. This extends the target projections into 2027.

  • Reactive Chasing: Analyst consensus target prices clearly lag behind actual stock price movements, reflecting momentum-chasing behavior.
  • Trailing Action: Analysts revise targets upward after a stock rises and downward after it falls, rather than serving as leading indicators.

Executive Conclusions & Findings

1. Inability to Predict Exponential Growth

For high-performing mega-caps (NVDA, AAPL, META, AVGO, LLY), analysts systematically underestimated the magnitude of expansion, resulting in high hit rates (60-84%) but negative MFEs. This suggests Wall Street models fail to capture the exponential tailwinds of AI and tech consolidation.

2. No Signal in Target Spreads

Because correlation and regression metrics are extremely weak, investors should not rely on target-implied returns (expected % returns) to rank stocks. A stock with a 50% target return is no more likely to outperform a stock with a 10% target return.

3. Targets as Lagging Indicators

Consensus target price changes represent a smoothed, lagging representation of recent stock momentum. Analysts adjust target prices primarily to stay aligned with the current market price rather than to offer independent leading signals.
